title: The three robbers
hook: Ramakrishna's three robbers in a forest, and the Gita's field marks for each guna
carry: tamas strikes, rajas binds, sattva shows the road

segments.voice: Yesterday: nature is woven of three gunas, sattva, rajas and tamas, twisted like one rope. Today, how to spot each one, and a story about where they leave you.

Ramakrishna, the nineteenth-century saint of Bengal, told this one. A traveler is crossing a forest when three robbers jump him and take everything. The first says: why keep him alive? and reaches for his knife. The second says: no, just tie him up. They tie him and walk off. Later the third comes back alone, unties him, says sorry, and walks him to the main road. That's your way home, he says. Come with me, the traveler begs. I can't, says the robber. The police would know me. The forest, Ramakrishna said, is this world. The three robbers are the gunas.
screen: `ONE REACHES FOR A KNIFE.` → `ONE TIES HIM UP.` → `ONE SHOWS HIM THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: In the Gita, Krishna gives Arjuna the field marks of the same three. Verse ten: one thread rises by pushing down the other two, so the mix is always shifting. Verse eleven: when light and understanding shine through every gate of the body, the eyes, the ears, the mind, sattva is strong. Verse twelve: greed, busyness, starting one project after another, restlessness, longing: that's rajas rising. Verse thirteen: darkness, sluggishness, carelessness, confusion: that's tamas. Verse seventeen follows each to where it leads: from sattva, knowledge; from rajas, greed; from tamas, confusion. Verse eighteen gives a direction: those in sattva rise, those in rajas stay in the middle, those in tamas sink. The chapter even says the thread you're in at the end of life shapes what comes next. Then verse nineteen: when the seer sees no doer other than the gunas, and knows what is beyond them, that one reaches my being. That's how Ramakrishna read the robbers. Tamas would destroy you, rajas ties you up, sattva unties you and points to the road, but even the kind robber can't walk you home. Home is beyond all three. And the first step is noticing: the moment you can say, oh, that's rajas, you're already a little outside it.
screen: `ONE RISES, TWO FALL.` · `LIGHT, GREED, OR FOG.` · `KNOWLEDGE, GREED, CONFUSION.` · `SATTVA SHOWS THE ROAD.` · then, large: `HOME IS BEYOND THE THREE.`

segments.voice: Scan yourself for the Gita's field marks. Light and clear seeing, through the eyes and ears: the bright thread. Restlessness, wanting, an itch in the hands to start something new: the moving thread. Fog, heaviness, a wish to go blank: the heavy one. Whatever is strongest, name it softly, the way Nani might: ah, that's rajas. Then rest as the one who noticed. The robbers move; the watcher isn't one of them.
Rajas, passion, motion, heat: the robber who ties you up. Gita fourteen, twelve: its marks are greed, busyness, starting one thing after another, restlessness and longing.
Your line: tamas strikes, rajas binds, sattva shows the road. Home is beyond all three. Two hundred eight days now.

howItsDone: Some Hindus use the gunas as a practical check on daily life, choosing food, company and routines that support sattva; some teachers use Gita 14.11–14.13 to describe what each guna looks like.

what a scholar hears: 14.10 describes each guna prevailing by overpowering the other two; 14.19 makes seeing the gunas as the only doers the doorway beyond them; Ramakrishna's parable of the three robbers is recorded in the Kathamrita (the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna).
